title: Towards Wholeness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes that spiritual growth and self-realization cannot be achieved by ignoring fundamental human needs, such as safety, love, and belonging. Rather, these needs must be acknowledged and addressed before one can focus on spiritual practice. By recognizing and meeting our basic needs, we create space for spiritual growth and self-awareness to emerge, rather than trying to suppress or avoid pain and suffering.
topics: Buddhist concept of an illusionary fixed self

sentences.text: Good evening everybody, nice to see you, familiar faces and less so, nice you could come.
I want to give a dharma talk.
Before I do, I wanted to make one point about zafu operations, how to operate a zafu.
If you're sitting in one of the cross-legged postures, it seems to work pretty well, and you can try this, to make sure you're sitting at the very front edge of the cushion.
If you're in the middle, you might want to lift your rear end up and slide yourself forward.

So you're sitting at the front edge of the cushion, and what happens is your pelvis tips forward a little bit and that creates the beginnings of a natural curve, so that you can really open the chest and extend the back of the spine gently, not straining but just feeling a gentle extension and rising up of the spine, and where the spine comes into the neck.
One thing that's nice to do, especially when you first sit down, is to emphasize that extension and opening on an inhalation.
So inhale and get nice and tall, and then on the exhalation just release tension.
Let go of the shoulders.
If you're holding in the chest or the belly, try to release that a little bit.
If the back is upright and the chest is open, it's easier for the breathing to operate.
So I just want to make that point.
You would think you'd sit in the middle of the thing, but I guess they make all the back parts so it can stick out in the air.
I don't know why it's all there.
I just sit on the front edge.
I wanted to speak tonight a little bit about wholeness and connection.
This talk is called Towards Wholeness, and hopefully it won't be too long.
I'm a little concerned that it's a bit long.
Since I've had an overly busy schedule for the last five or six or seven years, I developed the ability to write talks really fast.
I used to have an hour or two max to write a talk, and I'd whip out a 40-50 minute talk in an hour or two.
Today I had twice that much time.
I think I was probably moving at my usual speed, so I was just back there trying to chop it down a little bit.
If it is too long, please forgive me, and change your posture if it gets to be too painful to be sitting there.
The formal approach to Dharma talks is that it's just like another period of zazen.
So you can play with that a little bit.
We're not too worried about being too formal, but the formal idea is that it's not like there's information you need to learn, or take notes on, or remember.
It's just another way to be mindful, in the context of listening.
So you can try sitting in zazen posture, but if it gets to be too much, just be comfortable.
I wanted to bring up some teachings from a sutra called the Tathagata Garbha Sutra, and I also want to talk a little bit about psychology and about scientific studies of the mind and the body.
It's a huge agenda.
But really, what is all this about?
It's just about what it is to be a human being.
How do we do this, this being a human being, being a person?
Maybe all of human endeavor is about that question.
All of us here are basically more or less doing fine.
We probably have our basic physical needs met.

We probably all ate today, and yet I don't want to talk about how we can be happier without acknowledging that there are many millions, and maybe billions, of people in the world who probably didn't eat today.
So let's remember them as we consider how to live our life more happily and more fully in our fortunate circumstances.

The other thing about being a human being that the Buddha spoke about, and that Western psychology investigates, is that strangely, even though we all were able to eat today, we still have some problems.
People ourselves or people we know who are getting around and seem pretty much fine, and can smile and shake your hand and tell you they're fine, might not really be fine.
There might be some deep troubles and difficulties going on for them.
This comes and goes for all of us throughout our life.
If you are feeling particularly happy and balanced now, that's wonderful.
That's great.
But just wait.
Things will change.
And luckily the same is true of the reverse.
If you're having a really difficult time in your life, that'll change too.
So I want to start by thinking about psychology.
When you think about the psychology of human needs, and I'll have to ask the therapist later if psychology really agrees with this guy still, or ever did, I always think of Abraham Maslow.
He was the founder, posthumous founder I guess, of humanistic psychology.
He died in the early 70s, I think.
He created a wonderful hierarchy of needs, which I think is really applicable to us as practitioners.
Sometimes the way we approach spiritual practice is we think that we can leapfrog over some of the basic human needs.
Maybe it's okay if things aren't quite sorted out in our home life or this or that.
If we just do spiritual practice, we could skip all that and be happy.
It doesn't really seem to work that way.
So I want to remind us of Maslow's hierarchy of needs.
The way he described it, there's really a hierarchy.
One is satisfied and then you start to have needs in the next one, but it's probably a little more mixed together than that.
Whenever they make discrete categories, it's probably not quite that way.
His first need is our physiological needs, as I was mentioning.
Biological needs for oxygen, food, water, a healthy relationship to sexuality, a relatively constant body temperature.
Think about that.
Human beings can exist within about 20 degrees Fahrenheit.
We have such a narrow band that we can survive.
And these of course are the strongest needs, because if a person is deprived of all of them, they can't live.
So first we have physiological needs.
Then we have needs for safety, once the physiological needs are met.
These are needs for security.
Mostly we don't have too much awareness of our needs for security, except when there's trouble, in times of emergency or disorganization or when the social structure breaks down.
Children are often more sensitive to the need for safety, so you see this more in kids.
We are convinced that society is basically stable and we don't usually worry about this too much.
But you don't have to look very far in the news to know there are many places in the world where one's safety is not taken for granted like it is in Bellingham, Washington.
So that was the second one, needs for safety, and most of us are probably doing pretty well.
But then it starts to get a little more subtle.
The third one is our need for love, affection, and belonging.

*This next class of needs for love, affection, and belonging emerge once safety and physiological needs are met.* And Maslow states that *people seek to overcome their feelings of loneliness and alienation.* That's the need, to overcome loneliness and alienation.
*This requires giving and receiving love and affection and a strong sense of belonging.* I think we probably all would say, "Well, I pretty much have that."
But you can probably think of areas in your life that aren't quite the way you might like.
Or you don't quite feel that sense of belonging like you might like to feel.
Or you don't quite feel affection in the way you might like to.
So that was the third of the five.
The fourth need is the need for esteem.
It says here, *when the first three classes of needs are satisfied, the need for esteem can become dominant.
This involves the need for self-esteem and for the esteem and respect a person gets from others.* So we have a need to be validated and respected.
*Humans have a need for a stable, firmly based, high level of self-respect and respect from others.
When these needs are satisfied, a person feels self-confident and valuable as a person in the world.
When these needs are frustrated, a person feels inferior, weak, helpless, and worthless.* Again, I think it's not all or nothing.
I think we all have in a way a healthy self-esteem and plenty of esteem from others.
But there might be areas in our life where we realize, "I sometimes do feel some shade of inferior, weak, or helpless."
Maybe it's because there's not enough giving and receiving of esteem.
That's the fourth one.
The fifth one is the famous one, which I think he invented: the need for self-actualization.
Maslow describes self-actualization as *a person's need to be and do what that person is born to do.* So this is somehow touching on some deep need that you are born with, or somehow have developed.
He said, *a musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write.
These needs make themselves felt in signs of restlessness.
A person could feel on edge, tense, lacking something.
If a person is hungry, unsafe, not loved, accepting, or lacking self-esteem,* in those cases it's easy to know what a person is feeling restless about.
*It's not always clear what a person needs when there is a need for self-actualization.*
So this is somehow like attaining one's potential.
This is what children are wondering about when they think about what they want to be when they grow up, and grown-ups too, I guess.
Here it gets a little more subtle, and maybe spiritual practice intersects this pretty directly.
What do you really need to be actualized, to be fully yourself, one could say, or fully a person?
It's so easy to be confused, I think, about one's need for self-actualization.
We can confuse someone else's idea of what we need for self-actualization with what we actually need.
So this is a wonderful enlightened thing from psychology, I think.
I don't really know psychology, so later the psychologist can straighten me out.

One thing about all psychology is that it seems to assume that there is a self: a self to self-actualize, a self to have self-esteem, a self to interact with other independent selves to create these mutually supportive bonds that we need to achieve these five levels of need.
So on the face of it, there might appear to be some conflict between psychology and Buddhism, because, as you probably have heard, Buddhism is a little confusing.
Maybe you've heard this, but you ask your Buddhist friends and they're a little confused by it.
Buddhism seems to say, "Well, there actually isn't a self, you were mixed up about that."
A self does not actually exist in the way that you thought it did.
It's not solid and real and permanent.
Buddhism suggests that the self is a concept, a very powerful and well developed idea, a conceptual framework that we lay on top of our experience.
We impose it on top of a very complex set of psychophysical phenomena that we're perceiving all the time, probably a hundred billion perceptions per day.
Somehow we organize all that into the idea of a self so that we can function and make sense of the world.
Of course, the only way we can actually make this work, and cognitive psychology did some famous experiments and figured this out, is that we ignore most of the perceptions coming in.
We only let in the ones that make sense to our sense of self.
They can do these experiments where people completely don't perceive things because of the way their attention is working and the way they conceptualize.
I just read about a really good one.
I didn't write it down, but I forget what it was.
Somehow they got the subjects of this experiment involved and focused on one thing, and then they had this guy in a gorilla suit walk through the room and nobody saw him.
I forget how they got the person focused on something else, but it was that kind of thing.
You're doing something that makes sense to you and you're engaged in it, and someone in a gorilla suit walks through the room and you didn't even see it.
The photons must have hit your eyeballs, but it didn't get into your brain.
Anyway, Buddhism suggests that we don't just take this on faith.
Somebody's not telling us we don't exist; we should check it out with practice, with meditation practice and teachings and awareness practices.
Buddhism suggests some analytical tools, different ways that we can categorize and reconceptualize and notice more minutely and precisely what's really arising in each moment.

So instead of saying, "This is me walking down the street, perception of breeze on the face, perception of this, feeling of that, memory arising," we can start to peel things back to a moment-by-moment basis for experience.
Little by little we realize, well, there's not exactly a me there.
There are things happening, there are things being perceived, but is there really a me there?
Sooner or later you can't find anything that's a me, that's a you, that's a self.
And so therefore it might seem like Buddhism is saying, "Well, forget all about Maslow.
Why would you go to all this work to take care of yourself if it doesn't exist?"
And if you try that, you will really suffer, and you find out that that doesn't work either.
You can try that though, people do.
Usually at bigger centers, where it seems like it's really hardcore, people come and try to get rid of their self and they really suffer.

Because it turns out the only way that we can soften up about our self, because it's the rigidity of self that causes so much of our suffering, the only way we can really transcend and be soft and loose and gentle with our sense of self is if our sense of self is really in good shape, is really well taken care of.
If all five of Abraham Maslow's levels of self-actualization are really being met.
And like I was saying earlier, sometimes people think they can use spiritual practice as a shortcut.
But what happens as you do spiritual practice is that your self-awareness increases almost inevitably, no matter how so-called good or bad you are at it.
Things start to arise in the mind that maybe you hadn't thought about, or maybe you were ignoring or repressing.
And you start to notice the places where your need for self-actualization or your need for love and belonging, or even your need for safety, are not fully being met.
And you start to realize, "I can't ignore that anymore.
That's hurting me too much to not take care of my life fully.
I can't skip over what I need, even though there's not exactly a me that needs it."
It just works that way.
And what Buddhism is really interested in, on a moment-by-moment basis, is not what's right or what makes sense, but what causes suffering.
What causes joy and release of suffering?
And if you do some experiments in your life, you find that ignoring your basic human needs causes suffering, and so you have to attend to them.

So in a way, you can come to spiritual practice thinking, "I'm going to transcend the self," and realize through your spiritual practice that actually, you have to take much better care of yourself as part of your practice.

Now, psychology is also very interested in easing suffering, in analyzing how we came to have the different tendencies and issues and psychoses and neuroses and all kinds of [unclear: "C's"] that we have.
Buddhism is not so interested in figuring out why things happened as in carefully examining how they happen and what they really are.
And so we tend to say, "Pain and suffering, I don't want that.
I'm going to run as fast as possible or do whatever I can to suppress or avoid or remove that pain and suffering from my life."
But Buddhism suggests, well, why don't you not be so quick about that?
Why don't you stick around in pain and suffering for a minute and see what's really going on?
Maybe you can learn to engage and interact with pain and suffering in a more nuanced and intelligent way, and thus be more effective in reducing suffering in a meaningful and lasting way.
And so the Buddha came up with a theory from his practice, handed down to us over all these years, I guess, of three levels of suffering.
And suffering is maybe, it's sometimes hard to get these things to work out right in English.
They actually use phrases which have a common root.
And the root word is a Sanskrit word, dukkha.
It usually gets translated "suffering," but suffering sounds a little too big.
So these are the three levels of dukkha, three levels of suffering.
The first is called dukkha dukkha.
It's easier to remember that one, dukkha dukkha, which is the pain of pain.

So these are obvious pains: physical pain, illness, aging, and additionally psychological and mental suffering, when we're upset, when we don't like things, when things are not the way we want, when we're bereaved, when we're mad, when we're angry.
These are dukkha dukkha; immediate physical and emotional and psychological pain is dukkha dukkha.
And basically the understanding is that some amount of dukkha dukkha cannot be avoided, because you're a human being in a body with a mind.
It's just the way it goes.
But it turns out, if we look more carefully at what we think was dukkha dukkha, it's actually a whole mix of other things too.
On top of the physical pain are many other levels of experience, which we add to that experience to make it much worse for ourselves.
So it's useful to know about the second and third level of dukkha so that we can start little by little to distinguish.
For instance, you go on a long meditation retreat, there will definitely be some pain.
Sorry, just happens.
But then what you start to notice is, there's pain in the knee, but then on top of pain in the knee, I start to have anxiety, a sort of formless anxiety: "Is this good?
Is this bad?"
And then I start to wonder, "Am I causing permanent damage here?
Is this a masochistic thing?
Is this a [unclear: "crate"]?
What am I doing here?
Why am I at this retreat?
These other people are probably really, you know..."
And pretty soon you're in a much worse state than just the sensation in the knee.
And so what you're adding are these other levels of dukkha.
The second one is called the Viparanamma dukkha.
And this is the suffering born of change, the dukkha of change.
This is really important, actually, and something we're a little bit in denial of all the time.
We all know perfectly well that everything is changing, right?
We know that all of us are changing and every existing thing is changing and nothing is permanent.
But we don't really live as if we fully understood that.
We live as if there's always tomorrow, I can always get to it later, my friends and family will always be around.
And so it really shocks us when, seemingly suddenly, they get sick or they die.
But actually everyone's changing and everything's changing all the time.
And so the suffering born of change is our denial of that and resistance to that, our blindness to that, such that it seems to happen to us in these painful little gaps and starts.
Because we weren't watching it as it went gradually along, suddenly there's enough change that we notice again: "Oh my gosh, she's getting older.
How did that happen?
She wasn't older yesterday.
I didn't notice that."
And so the Buddha taught a lot about fully engaging our understanding of the complete changing nature of all phenomena, and that if we ignore that or deny that, there's a lot of suffering.
So that's the second level of dukkha.
And the third level of dukkha is a little more subtle yet.
This is called samskara dukkha.
To explain samskara dukkha, I have to explain the word samskara and talk a little bit about Buddhist psychology.
Samskaras are conditioned things, assembled things, things that come together from other things.
In other words, samskaras are basically all phenomena that we can perceive.
So when you get angry, some combination of factors is coming together in your mind and anger arises.
When a seed is planted, some combination of factors in genetics and water and sun and all these things come together and a plant grows.
And these things happen.
And you can take any psychophysical thing.
Buddhism doesn't make so much of the distinction that we do between physical things and mental objects.
And if you look at it carefully, you can see it's made of other things, right?
Like atoms, molecules.
What's inside a molecule?
What's inside a atom?
What's inside that?
And so how does that connect to suffering?
You might ask him.
Is Buddhist saying that everything that exists is going to cause suffering?
That doesn't sound like very good news.
What he's saying is something like, when we see objects, it's connected to the second one.
When we interact with mental and physical objects, we interact with them as if they had intrinsic reality.
And we think they can be depended on in a certain kind of way, and we depend on them to give ourselves happiness and satisfaction.
And what he's saying is that actually the nature of all existent things is that they are constantly coming and going and reforming and changing.
It's a more subtle and fuller version of the second level: that everything that exists has a quality of fluidity, and more than impermanence, a kind of impermanence beyond impermanence.
And so one way to think about this kind of suffering is the way that we go around trying to make sense of things.
Like you hear about people trying to find a better balance in their life.
I've been working on that.
I've been trying to find a better balance in my life.
We're constantly trying to conceptualize and make sense of things as if they were existent and solid.
And what the Buddha is saying is that things are so much more radically fluid than that.
So whenever we try to make sense of things in a way that our happiness hinges on, we're going to be let down.
Things are going to turn out to be a little different than we thought.
They're going to change.
Things are going to die.
Things are going to be not what we thought.
Everything's going to rearrange.
It's almost like you try to make sense of things and things settle down in your mind.
And we've all had this experience: you're going along fine, then something happens and it's like, I don't know, you're like a snow globe or something.
Someone just shook you all up again.
It's like there's a blizzard and you can't see what's happening anymore, you know what I mean?
So that's one way.
It's a little bit hard to talk about the third level of suffering.
It's the suffering born of a limited view of reality, I suppose, is one way to look at it.
And it's the suffering that can't really be engaged with by thinking or conceptualizing.
It's a suffering that's engaged with directly through spiritual practice.
So these are three levels of dukkha.
Simple pain, dukkha dukkha; pain from suffering from change, vipara nama dukkha; and this more subtle suffering of existence and our misunderstanding of existence, which is samskara dukkha.

So I think the interaction between Maslow's hierarchy of needs and Buddha's teaching of these three levels of suffering seems to be one way to look at it: even if your Maslowian hierarchy of needs was well met, this is where it gets interesting and why there is spiritual practice.
So you've got food in your belly.
You've got love in your heart, your confidence in yourself and your abilities, and you're doing what's most deeply fulfilling to you and all your relationships are wholesome and wonderful.
It's funny that saying that sounds like a joke.
Why does that sound like a joke to us?
It's kind of sad, isn't it?
Why would that not be our natural state as human beings?
But anyway, let's assume that that was fully possible.
Everything was great.
And yet there's still some sense there, you know what I mean?
Even when everything's going great, there's still some sense of something not being quite it.

And I think human beings have tremendous abilities to get busy and occupied and ignore that feeling, that niggling feeling at the back of your neck, the hairs in the back of the neck just twitching a little bit, even though it's a wonderful evening and you're having a wonderful time with your partner and everything's just perfect.
But there's just, you know what I mean?
This little sense of dis-ease.
So why is that?
That's where samskara dukkha is helpful.
It helps us to have some concept to work with what's really nonconceptual, so that we can turn towards that and eventually, through our practice, put that to rest too.
So we can let ourselves off the hook a little bit: "Well, of course I feel a little dis-ease, or samskara dukkha, just everywhere.
No big deal, I can work with this."
Because from a psychology point of view, and a human point of view, without those teachings it seems like we're broken, you know what I mean?
The machine is getting all it needs, it should be running perfectly, but there's a little catch in the mechanism.
The human machine must be broken somehow.
And that really is upsetting.
So it helps to have some teachings and some way to engage with very subtle levels of dis-ease.
As I understand it, conventional psychology drops off at that point.
Perfect unconditional happiness is out of scope for psychology, and I don't mean to belittle psychology.
I think it's naturally a human science, and it just can't go that far.
Psychology, I think, is interested in people becoming reasonably happy, which would be great.
It would be wonderful if everyone in the world were reasonably happy, well adjusted, and maybe a little resigned to the little problems of life.
Just basically okay, right?
I'm okay, you're okay.
So I think spirituality has something to add, but it cannot ignore psychology.
That would be a mistake.
And psychology also, so far, most mainline branches of psychology are not very concerned in a direct way with our physical presence.
I'm sure your therapist might suggest it would probably be a good idea to exercise, but they're not intimately involved with your physicality.
Psychology is interested in the mind: how we think, how emotions and thoughts interact, how our history colors and conditions our thinking, and so on.
If there's a physical problem, you should go to the doctor.
Science, of course, by its nature, has great power in specificity, in looking carefully at one thing.
So it is very compartmentalized.
Its great power is a focused inquiry into one area with one set of tools.
And so psychology just doesn't really have the tools to engage with the body, and doctors don't really have the tools to engage with psychology.
Neither of them seems to be engaging with something beyond that.
So, continuing on a science kick for a minute, I thought we'd look at an interesting area of science that I've been reading about a little bit lately, which ties these things together.
Science is not oblivious to these connections.
I want to tell you a little bit about behavioral medicine.
It's not really the best name.
It sounds like the medicine of how you behave or something like that.
But behavioral medicine is concerned with how people's thinking and attitudes affect their health.
It's been active research since the sixties, so it's not a new thing.
But strangely, some of the things that are very clear from behavioral medicine studies, and that would really affect our happiness, we do not take to heart.
So I want to bring up a few of those things and then get back to Buddhism.
Then hopefully there'll be time for discussion.
We'll see.
I did not do an exhaustive review of the scientific literature today, obviously, but I did read some things about behavioral medicine in a book by Jon Kabat-Zinn called Full Catastrophe Living.

He starts out his section on behavioral medicine by telling a really powerful story, told to him by a man named Bernard Loewen, who is a cardiologist, about something that happened to him when he was in his training.
Here's what Bernard Loewen said he saw when he was a young med student.
This is really interesting.
*This experience still provokes in me a shudder of disbelief.
Some thirty years ago, I had a post-doctorate fellowship with Dr.
S.
A.
Levine, professor of cardiology at the Harvard Medical School.
He was a keen observer of the human scene.
He had an awesome presence, was precise in formulation, and was blessed with a prodigious memory.
He was, in fact, a consummate clinician at the bedside.
Dr.
Levine conducted a weekly outpatient cardiac clinic at the hospital.
After we young trainees examine the patient,*
So people are coming in to get looked at who have some kind of heart condition.
*after we young trainees examine the patient, he would drop in briefly to assess our findings and suggest further diagnostic workup or changes in our therapeutic program.
With patients, he was invariably reassuring and convincing, and they venerated him and listened to his every word.
In one of my very first clinics, I had as a patient Mrs.
S., a well-preserved middle-aged librarian who had a narrowing in one of the valves on the right side of her heart, the tricuspid valve.
She had been in a low grade congestive heart failure with a modest edema, a swelling of the ankles, for years, but was able to maintain her job and attend efficiently to her household.
She was receiving digitalis and weekly injections of a mercurial diuretic.
Dr.
Levine, who had followed her in the clinic for more than a decade,*
So she's known, she's had this condition for more than a decade, working with this doctor.
*greeted Mrs.
S. warmly and then turned to the large entourage of visiting physicians and said, "This woman has T.S." and abruptly left.
No sooner was Dr.
Levine out the door than Mrs.
S.'s demeanor abruptly changed.
She appeared anxious suddenly and frightened.
She was now breathing rapidly, clearly hyperventilating.
Her skin was drenched with perspiration and her pulse had accelerated to more than 150 beats a minute.
In reexamining her, I found it astonishing that the lungs, which a few minutes earlier had been quite clear, now had moist crackles at the bases.
This was extraordinary, for with obstruction of the right heart valve, the lungs are spared the accumulation of excess fluid.*
That shouldn't have been happening.
*I questioned Mrs.
S. as to the reasons for her sudden upset.
Her response was that Dr.
Levine had said that she had T.S., which she said she knew meant terminal situation.

I was initially amused at this misinterpretation of the medical acronym for tricuspid stenosis, but my amusement quickly yielded to apprehension, as my words of explanation failed to reassure her, and her congestion continued to worsen.
Shortly thereafter, she was in massive pulmonary edema,*
So, a big heart attack.
*Heroic measures did not reverse the frothing congestion in her heart.
I tried to reach Dr.
Levine, but he was nowhere to be located.
Later that same day, she died from intractable heart failure.
To this day, the recollection of this tragic happening causes me to tremble at the awesome power of the physician's word.*
And you could also say the awesome power of anybody's word, the power of words and thinking.
So I might skip over some of the many studies I had written down to tell you about, because that one example kind of tells it all, in a way.
But they've done many studies, placebo studies you've heard of, where one group gets the medication, both groups are told what the medication does, and half of them get a sugar pill.
It's been shown over and over again that the people getting the sugar pill show some of the same effects of the drug, every time.
Sometimes that effect approaches the actual levels of the people who got the real drug.
So how could that be?
Regular medicine can't explain that.
There are also studies about optimistic and pessimistic people.
They have to define these terms, but basically happier, more optimistic people are much less likely to get cancer, to get heart failure, to get all kinds of diseases.
This has been established.
They've also established that people with a strong feeling of connection to others are much less likely to get major diseases, including cancer.
And if you do get cancer, your feeling of connection and optimism seems to greatly influence, or correlates with, a much better survival rate.
They don't really know how positive attitude correlates with it.
One can't talk about behavioral medicine without bringing up Type A.
We've all heard of Type A, so I was excited to finally find out what Type A was about.
Maybe you all know this.
Elizabeth went to med school, maybe I told her about it.
So it turns out, I'll tell you about Type A.
You've got to know about it, then you can be more accurate about what Type A was about.
It was about the early fifties, and it gained a lot of credibility from a large study in the early 1960s in England, I think, of a large group of men.
They grouped these men into Type A and Type B personality types.
Type A is people driven by a lot of urgency: competitive, hostile, aggressive, maybe with some sense of insecurity.
Type B is more contemplative and relaxed.
